यह पुस्तक माता-पिता, माताओं, दादा-दादी, शिक्षकों और देखभाल करने वालों के लिए सामान्य शैक्षिक मार्गदर्शन के लिए लिखी गई है। यह चिकित्सा सलाह, निदान, उपचार, विकासात्मक मूल्यांकन, भाषण चिकित्सा, व्यावसायिक चिकित्सा, मनोवैज्ञानिक देखभाल या आपातकालीन देखभाल को प्रतिस्थापित नहीं करता है।

हर बच्चा अलग तरह से बढ़ता है। इस पुस्तक में दिए गए मार्गदर्शन का उद्देश्य परिवारों को विकास का निरीक्षण करने, दैनिक विकास का समर्थन करने और चेतावनी के संकेत दिखाई देने पर शीघ्र सहायता प्राप्त करने में मदद करना है। यदि किसी बच्चे को दौरे पड़ते हैं, सांस लेने में कठिनाई होती है, गंभीर कमजोरी होती है, निर्जलीकरण होता है, कौशल में अचानक कमी आती है, गंभीर चोट लगती है, बार-बार उल्टी होती है, असामान्य व्यवहार के साथ तेज बुखार होता है, या इस पुस्तक में चर्चा किए गए किसी भी खतरे के संकेत पर, तुरंत चिकित्सा देखभाल लें।

How to Use This Book

Many mothers worry without knowing what is normal and what is not. Some mothers ignore signs that need early help. This book will help you know what is common, what needs attention, what you can do at home, and when you should go to the doctor. A mother who understands her child can protect the child’s future with love and wisdom.

Chapter 4 — A Child Needs Love, Food, Sleep, and Play

A small child does not grow by food alone. A child needs four big things every day: love, food, sleep, and play. If one of these is weak, growth may suffer. A child who gets food but no love may become fearful, angry, or quiet. A child who gets love but poor food may become weak. A child who sleeps badly may become irritable and slow in learning. A child who never plays may miss many chances to grow. Love makes the child feel safe. Good food builds body and brain. Sleep gives rest, repair, and fresh energy. Play teaches movement, speech, thinking, confidence, and friendship. These are not small things. These are the real pillars of childhood. A mother does not need costly things for this. Warm words, simple healthy food, regular sleep, and daily play are enough. A child grows best in a home where there is care, routine, patience, and laughter. These simple daily gifts help build a strong future.

Feelings are also part of development. A child learns not only alphabets and numbers but also waiting, sharing, losing, apologizing, asking for help, and calming down after anger. These skills grow slowly. A mother should name feelings in simple words: angry, sad, scared, happy, tired, hurt. When a feeling gets a name, the child slowly learns to control it.

At home, correct behavior without crushing the child. Be firm about hitting, lying, unsafe behavior, and disrespect, but do not insult the child as bad, useless, or shameful. Praise small good actions. Notice if the child is always withdrawn, always aggressive, always frightened, or suddenly very different from before. Emotional warning signs deserve care as much as physical signs.

Chapter 5 — How the Brain Grows in Early Childhood

A child’s brain grows very fast in early years. This growth does not happen by itself alone. The brain grows better when the child hears words, sees faces, feels safe, plays, touches things, and gets love. Every day, the child’s brain learns from small experiences. When the mother talks, sings, smiles, and responds, the brain becomes more active and strong. The brain helps the child speak, remember, understand, move, and control feelings. Good food helps the brain. Good sleep helps the brain. Play helps the brain. Peace at home also helps the brain. Too much fear, shouting, neglect, or screen time can disturb healthy brain growth. A mother may not see the brain, but she can shape it daily. A child who is spoken to, played with, and cared for learns faster. A child who is always ignored or left only with mobile may fall behind. Early years are precious. The brain is growing quietly every day. A mother’s care becomes part of that growth.

Brain growth is helped by curiosity, repetition, sleep, food, play, and calm guidance. The child should be allowed to ask, try, fail, and try again. Learning is not only copying from a book. Counting fruits, sorting clothes, remembering small instructions, telling a story, helping arrange objects, and asking why and how are all brain exercises.

A mother should observe whether the child is improving slowly. One weak day is not a disease, but a repeated pattern needs attention. If the child cannot remember simple things, cannot follow two small steps, avoids all learning, cries every time study begins, or falls far behind in school, the solution is not beating. The solution is patient teaching, teacher discussion, and early assessment when needed.

Chapter 6 — How Talking Helps a Child Grow

Talking to a child is one of the simplest and strongest ways to help development. Many mothers think, "He is small, what will he understand?" But even a small child learns from hearing daily words. When the mother talks during feeding, bathing, walking, dressing, and play, the child slowly learns sounds, words, meaning, and connection. Talking helps speech. It also helps brain growth, memory, listening, and bonding. A child learns names of people, foods, body parts, animals, and actions. He learns how to ask, answer, and express feelings. Even if the child cannot reply well, he is still learning. That is why silence around a child is not good. Use simple words. Repeat often. Name things around the house. Sing songs. Tell little stories. Ask small questions. Wait for the child to answer. Do not laugh at wrong speech. Help gently. A child whose family talks warmly and regularly often grows better in speech and confidence. Talking is free, but its value is very great.

Speech grows when the child hears warm human language again and again. Mobile sounds and television words do not replace a mother's face, tone, pause, and response. Speak slowly, name objects, describe daily actions, read picture books, sing short songs, and give the child time to answer. Do not correct every word harshly. Gentle repetition works better.

At home, make a small rule that important times are speech times: meals, bath, dressing, walking, and bedtime. Ask simple questions and wait. If the child does not respond to name, does not understand simple instructions, speaks very little for age, cannot be understood, or seems not to hear well, seek help early. Speech delay should not be hidden by shame.

Chapter 8 — Mobile, TV, and Screen Harm

Mobile and TV may keep a child quiet for some time, but too much screen can harm development. Many families give mobile during meals, crying, or free time. Slowly the child becomes dependent on it. Then speech may reduce, eye contact may reduce, sleep may worsen, anger may increase, and play may decrease. The child starts watching more and living less. A small child needs people more than screens. He needs face-to-face talk, touch, movement, outdoor play, stories, songs, and real objects. Screen cannot replace these. Fast-moving videos can also make the child restless, impatient, and less interested in normal life. This does not mean every screen is poison. But too much daily screen, especially in early years, is not good. Never use mobile as the main friend of the child. Keep mealtime, bedtime, and playtime free from screen. A mother should remember this simple truth: children grow by talking, touching, moving, and playing, not by staring at a screen for long hours.

Screens become harmful when they replace people, play, sleep, food routine, and outdoor life. A small child who spends long hours watching fast videos may become less patient with normal life. He may demand screen during meals, cry when it is removed, sleep late, speak less, or lose interest in real toys and people.

At home, do not remove the screen suddenly with anger if the child is already dependent. Reduce slowly and replace it with something real: blocks, balls, drawing, water play, story, song, outdoor walk, or helping in the kitchen safely. Keep meal time and bedtime screen-free. Parents must also reduce their own screen use because children copy what they see more than what they are told.

Chapter 9 — What Is Common and What Is Serious

Many things in childhood are common. Tantrums are common. Fussy eating is common. Bedwetting can be common. Thumb sucking can be common. Fear of darkness, strangers, or school can also happen. Small mistakes, crying, stubbornness, and fighting with siblings are often part of growing up. So a mother should not panic over every small issue. But some things are more serious. A child not hearing properly, not speaking at all, not making eye contact, not understanding simple words, losing skills already learned, having repeated fits, being very weak, or showing very unusual behavior may need doctor help early. Severe sadness, no play, no response, or major school difficulty also should not be ignored. The wise way is this: do not fear every common problem, but do not dismiss important signs. Watch carefully. Notice patterns. Ask, "Is this small and improving, or is it serious and continuing?" A calm mother who observes well can protect the child from both useless fear and dangerous delay.

A wise mother learns to separate common childhood difficulties from warning signs. Crying, stubbornness, fussy food, small fears, sibling fights, and occasional school dislike can be part of growth. But a continuing problem, a worsening problem, or a problem that stops normal life should not be ignored.

Keep a small note of what you see: when it started, how often it happens, what triggers it, and whether the child is improving or worsening. Seek help early for loss of skills, repeated fits, severe weakness, speech delay, poor eye contact, no response to name, severe school failure, breathing trouble, dehydration, serious injury, or a sudden major change in behavior. Early help protects the future.
